channel.title: Bhavesh Jain — Writing
channel.description: AI/ML, product development, and strategic foresight.

item.title: Before You Add an LLM, Build the Simplest Useful Baseline
item.description: Compare a proposed AI feature with search, rules, and a manual workflow before paying for complexity that users may not need.

item.title: Designing a Latency Budget for AI Features
item.description: Measure time to a useful result, trace the critical path, and reduce waiting without quietly removing the checks that make the answer dependable.

item.title: Build Versus Buy Is an Ownership Decision
item.description: Compare the full operating responsibility of a capability, including integration, support, change, and exit—not just development effort against a subscription.

item.title: RAG, Fine-Tuning, or Neither? Start with the Failure
item.description: Choose retrieval, prompt changes, fine-tuning, or a deterministic workflow by diagnosing the task failure—not by following an architecture trend.

item.title: Data Contracts: The Less Glamorous Side of Reliable ML
item.description: Define units, timestamps, ownership, and failure behavior at data boundaries so a valid-looking input cannot silently change the meaning of a prediction.

item.title: Product Discovery Before the Backlog Gets Expensive
item.description: Investigate the task, workaround, and consequence before turning a feature request into months of delivery work.

item.title: Product Experiments When You Don't Have Huge Traffic
item.description: Match the method to the uncertainty: use qualitative work for understanding, controlled experiments for causal questions, and honest limits when data is sparse.

item.title: Human Review Is a Workflow, Not a Checkbox
item.description: Make AI review actionable with evidence, realistic capacity, clear authority, and a measured path from correction to a completed task.

item.title: ML Monitoring After Launch: From Dashboards to Decisions
item.description: Separate service health, data quality, model outcomes, and user impact—and give each alert an owner and an action.

item.title: An MVP Should Complete One Workflow
item.description: Reduce the breadth of a first release without removing the beginning, ending, and recovery steps that make it useful.

item.title: Turning Product Feedback into Decisions, Not Just Tickets
item.description: Preserve the problem behind a request, compare evidence across users, and prioritize changes without treating request volume as a complete roadmap.

item.title: Product Metrics That Change a Decision
item.description: Choose a small set of outcome, diagnostic, and guardrail measures with explicit denominators and a clear reason to act.

item.title: Treat Prompt Changes Like Software Releases
item.description: Version prompts with their dependencies, evaluate changed behavior, and use controlled rollouts and rollback paths instead of editing production instructions in place.

item.title: From Prototype to Product: The Work Around the Demo
item.description: A useful prototype tests an assumption. A usable product also needs ownership, permissions, recovery, observability, and an honest delivery path.

item.title: When an AI Product Should Say “I Don't Know”
item.description: Design uncertainty as a useful next step: distinguish missing evidence, ambiguous requests, insufficient confidence, and unavailable capabilities.

item.title: From Black Box to Glass Box: Why Multi-Agent Systems Need to Show Their Work
item.description: Make AI systems inspectable with source evidence, action histories, and recovery controls—not a polished story about hidden reasoning.

item.title: What Air Cargo Forecasting Taught Me About Real-World ML
item.description: Lessons from the air-cargo forecasting problem: honest baselines, time-aware validation, decision-relevant errors, and an operational handoff.

item.title: Building a Trend Radar with LLMs (Without Hallucinating the Future)
item.description: A source-led design for trend discovery: collect evidence, test candidate signals, and use language models to explain rather than invent the story.

item.title: How to Actually Evaluate an LLM Application
item.description: Build evaluation around user tasks, separate development from holdout data, and make release decisions from evidence rather than a single score.

item.title: What a Trend Radar Actually Does in a Boardroom
item.description: Connect technology signals to decisions, accountable owners, and review dates instead of treating a radar chart as the strategy itself.

item.title: Why RAG Isn't a Silver Bullet
item.description: Retrieval helps an answer find evidence, but authority, permissions, coverage, and unsupported synthesis remain separate engineering problems.

item.title: Bibliometrics for Beginners: Reading Research Signals Carefully
item.description: Use publication and citation data to investigate research activity while accounting for coverage, age, field differences, and naming drift.

item.title: Notes from Building Multi-Agent Eval Harnesses
item.description: Evaluate agent workflows at the task, trace, and side-effect levels, with reproducible fixtures and explicit limits on retries and tool use.

item.title: Strategic Foresight vs Forecasting: They're Not the Same
item.description: Forecasting estimates defined outcomes; foresight explores plausible changes and strategic options. Useful decisions often need both.

item.title: The Quiet Cost of Average Accuracy
item.description: Use segment counts, error consequences, and calibrated uncertainty to understand what an attractive average can hide.

item.title: The Patent Signal: What Filings Quietly Reveal
item.description: Read patent activity as evidence of technical and organizational interest, with publication delays, family duplication, and commercialization limits in view.

item.title: Production Time Series in 2026: The Boring Tools That Win
item.description: A practical forecasting stack starts with baselines, honest backtests, input checks, and recovery—not a claim that one model family always wins.

item.title: Designing for the 10-Year Question
item.description: Use long-horizon questions to test assumptions, preserve options, and define signals that would change a decision—not to pretend the future is known.
